solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: No longer in — went out?

definitions.meaning: went out with someone, as on a romantic outing

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a person who is no longer at home has gone out.
explanation.definitionFit: Old-fashioned things are past their time, and a couple who went out together had a romantic engagement.

clue.text: Unexpectedly produces fences in the morning for building protection

indicators.note: fences enclose a space, so the rearranged letters surround the morning abbreviation
something done unexpectedly comes out in a surprising form, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: AM, ante meridiem, marks the morning

explanation.surface: Someone surprisingly puts up fences early in the day to protect a building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fences' reads as a noun the anagram produces, but it is the verb meaning encloses, and 'in the morning' is the abbreviation that gets enclosed.
explanation.definitionFit: A damp-proof layer set in a wall near ground level protects a building from rising moisture.

clue.text: Money box, perhaps

definitions.meaning: a metal container is one kind of box

explanation.surface: A money box is a child's savings container, hinted at as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang cash is called by this metal's name, and a can made of it is a sort of box.

clue.text: Club player, runner given the bird

parts.note: a river runs, and the Dee is a British river
the jay is a bird of the crow family

explanation.surface: A club sportsman, a runner, is given a bird of some kind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'runner' is the crossword convention for a river; 'Club' is a nightclub, not a sports club.
explanation.definitionFit: A disc jockey plays records in a nightclub, so is a player of music there.

clue.text: Case in college covered, keep running off copies for university

indicators.note: the outer letters are covered by the printing phrase, which goes round them

parts.note: to keep running off copies is to print on, carry on printing

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outside, so its first and last letters are taken

explanation.surface: A college case is hushed up while someone keeps printing copies for a university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case in' takes CE, the outside of 'college', and 'covered' wraps PRINT ON round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Princeton is an Ivy League university in New Jersey, USA.

clue.text: Bag to put in glass for Italian bread

indicators.note: the bag and the word to are put into the window glass

parts.note: a pane is a sheet of window glass
to net is to catch or bag

explanation.surface: An instruction to bag something and put it in a glass for some Italian bread.
explanation.definitionFit: Panettone is a sweet Italian loaf with dried fruit, eaten at Christmas.

clue.text: Bury every other part of pig, not bear

indicators.note: every other letter is taken, here the second, fourth and so on of the three words

explanation.surface: Someone is told to bury every other bit of a pig but not a bear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bury' looks like the Lancashire town but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To inter a body is to lay it in a grave, a formal synonym for burial.

clue.text: Recording put in class

indicators.note: the word for put goes in the word for class

parts.note: a caste is a hereditary social class
to set is to put or place

explanation.surface: A recording is played to a class at school.
explanation.definitionFit: A tape cassette holds an audio recording, so names the recording by its medium.

clue.text: Steal diamonds, perhaps — is that smart?

parts.note: British slang: to trouser money is to pocket it, often dishonestly
diamonds is one of the four suits of cards

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether stealing diamonds is clever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smart' looks like clever but means well dressed: the question asks whether the outfit is smart attire.
explanation.definitionFit: A matching jacket and trousers for women is formal wear, a smart outfit.

clue.text: Born and died in poverty

parts.note: née, French for born, introduces a married woman's maiden name
d is the standard abbreviation for died in genealogies

explanation.surface: Someone was born and died poor.
explanation.definitionFit: Need means want or destitution, a near synonym for being poor.

clue.text: Seed initially knocked into gravy, someone out to lunch?

indicators.note: the initial letter goes into the word for gravy

parts.note: gravy is slang for easy money

indicators.note: only the first letter of knocked is used

parts.note: a person who is out to lunch is crazy, a nut

explanation.surface: A seed is knocked into the gravy by someone not paying attention.
explanation.definitionFit: The peanut is the seed of a legume, called by this name in Britain.

clue.text: Accessory committed crime

definitions.meaning: a scarf or wrap worn over the shoulders

explanation.surface: An accessory to a crime, an accomplice, has committed it.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoulder wrap is a fashion accessory, and the past tense of the verb for thieving is the same word.

clue.text: Flat not having received letter?

definitions.meaning: a letter is a character, so this is being without one

explanation.surface: A flat, an apartment, has not had any post delivered.
explanation.definitionFit: Something flat and dull has no personality, and a written character is a letter.

clue.text: A day in tears, desperate to reach peak in Scotland

indicators.note: the day goes in among the rearranged letters
in a desperate state, out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: Thurs is the short form of Thursday

explanation.surface: Someone spends a day in tears, desperate to climb a Scottish summit.
explanation.walkthrough: The day goes in after the first letter of the rearranged weeping; 'to reach' is only a link. The hill overlooks Edinburgh.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur's Seat is the hill above Edinburgh, a well-known Scottish summit.

clue.text: Tablets help cut to be put right — good luck!

indicators.note: putting things right means rearranging them into order, so these letters are rearranged
a cut word loses its tail, so the last letter is removed

explanation.surface: A pharmacist hands over tablets to cure someone and wishes them luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut' trims HELP to HEL, which joins TABLETS in the letters that 'put right' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: A farewell wishing someone success is an idiom equal to wishing them luck.

clue.text: Nothing to add to it, bet not opening till

indicators.note: the round letter for nothing is added after the trimmed bet
the first letter, the opening, is dropped

parts.note: a punt is a bet
O, the round figure zero

explanation.surface: A gambler has nothing to add to a bet until later.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are archaic prepositions meaning up to or until, as in 'unto this day'.

clue.text: Security pass on the side

parts.note: a col is a mountain pass
lateral means at the side

explanation.surface: A security pass is worn on the side of a jacket.
explanation.definitionFit: Assets pledged against a loan are its security, guaranteeing repayment.

clue.text: Plain-living females wrapping old cape in tissue?

indicators.note: the tissue word is wrapped round the old cape, as in wrapping something in tissue

parts.note: a tissue of lies is a web of untruths, so the question mark asks for the falsehoods
a ness is a headland, a cape

explanation.surface: Austere women are wrapping an antique cape in tissue paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plain-living' is not frugal but living on the plains of Africa; 'in' simply joins 'wrapping' to its wrapper.
explanation.definitionFit: Female big cats of the African savannah live on grassy plains, so they are plains dwellers.

clue.text: Fox let hair down further?

definitions.meaning: to fox someone is to baffle them
letting one's hair down more is being more uninhibited

explanation.surface: A fox is asked to relax even more.
explanation.definitionFit: To fox means to confuse, and read as two words the answer says 'be more unrestrained'.

clue.text: Music maker hit on lover

indicators.note: in an across answer the hit word comes on, after, the lover

parts.note: a squeeze is slang for a boyfriend or girlfriend
to box is to punch

explanation.surface: A musician hits on their partner.
explanation.definitionFit: An accordion or concertina is a musical instrument, informally named for its bellows.

clue.text: American behind subject of joke

explanation.surface: An American is behind the subject of a joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Americans call the bottom by this word, and the person mocked is the target of the joke.

clue.text: Appropriate, top walls in gold

indicators.note: to wall something in is to enclose it, so the top word goes round the gold

parts.note: the brow is the top of a hill
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A suitable top encloses some gold.
explanation.definitionFit: To appropriate is to take for one's own use, a verb sense close to taking on loan.

clue.text: Guts shown by that woman quaffing drink in party game

indicators.note: courage is shown by the woman, so it follows her
the woman drinks, taking the drink inside her

parts.note: she is that woman
a pint is a drink of beer
British slang: bottle means nerve or courage

explanation.surface: A brave woman downs a drink during a party game.
explanation.definitionFit: A kissing game is played at parties, with players rotating a bottle to pick a partner.

clue.text: Trunks, rarely twisting, on being removed from the bottom

indicators.note: the word on is taken off the end, the bottom of a down entry

parts.note: torsion is twisting

explanation.surface: Trunks are seldom twisted while being removed from someone's bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rarely' belongs to the definition: the usual plural is 'torsos'.
explanation.definitionFit: Human trunks are the bodies without limbs, and this Latinate plural is the uncommon form.

clue.text: Party hosted by club, a shindig

indicators.note: the letters are hosted, held within, the words that follow

explanation.surface: A club holds a lively party.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally, a lively celebration is called by this word, a synonym of party.

clue.text: A thinker showing me the way?

parts.note: the head is the part that thinks

explanation.surface: A thinker leads the speaker along the right path.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone in front of you is leading, and leading is showing you the route.

clue.text: After pranging car, refuse cover again

indicators.note: British slang: to prang a car is to crash it, so these letters are smashed into a new order

explanation.surface: After crashing their car, someone refuses to drive again.
explanation.definitionFit: To lay a new top layer on a road is to put a fresh covering on it.

clue.text: Wizard, one in a suit

definitions.meaning: the card with value one in each suit of a pack

explanation.surface: A wizard is one man wearing a suit.
explanation.definitionFit: A brilliant performer is called an expert or star, and each suit of cards has a one-spot card.

clue.text: Most Irish jigs unreliable

indicators.note: a jig is a lively dance, so the letters jig about into a new order

explanation.surface: Most Irish dances are performed erratically.
explanation.definitionFit: Something haphazard sometimes succeeds and sometimes fails, so cannot be relied on.

clue.text: Cereal ending on blouse, I'm sorry about that!

indicators.note: the exclamation goes about, round, the final letter

parts.note: asking 'what?' is like saying 'sorry?' when you did not catch something

indicators.note: only the last letter of blouse is used

explanation.surface: Someone apologises for spilling cereal on a blouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that' only links the exclamation to the clue's end.
explanation.definitionFit: A staple grain crop used for flour, one of the main cereals.
